Nothing is debated until somebody introduces the text, because introduction is what puts a specific document before the chamber; the committee stage exists to examine that document and to let outside interests give evidence, and the chamber's vote comes on whatever the committee reports; and only after passage does the bill go to the head of state, whose signature is the act that makes an approved bill operative rather than merely agreed. questions.explanation: The rule exists to make a decision reachable. A chamber where any member can prevent a vote by keeping the debate alive can be held indefinitely by a determined opposition, so a closure motion that needs a specified majority in the chamber as a whole lets a side that commands three-fifths of all members end the discussion and proceed to the vote. It is not a speaking-time rule, which would constrain the member and not the outcome, and the speaker administers the procedure rather than deciding it, since it is the chamber that votes. Nor does closing a debate withdraw the right to amend in general: the specified majority remains in place for the amendments, which are simply voted on together with the question.

questions.explanation: Two constraints bind and the smaller decides. The floor has 42 days and needs 3 a bill, and 42 divided by 3 is exactly 14 bills. The committees together have 30 days and need 2 a bill, and 30 divided by 2 is 15, so there is committee capacity for one more bill than the floor can carry. The chamber therefore runs out of floor time first and completes 14, with the last bill's committee stage finishing while the floor is already full. Fifteen comes from looking only at the stage that ended with a day to spare, a bill cannot run through both stages on the same day, and nothing in the figures reserves 6 of the 42 floor days.

questions.explanation: The value of a fixed occasion is that it cannot be avoided. It is not chiefly a convenience about debate, because the point is the public accounting rather than the saving of time, and the written-answer route complements the session instead of replacing inquiry, since one gives a considered reply on the record and the other gives an immediate one. questions.explanation: The three features are what separate an inquiry from a debate. A written mandate fixes the question so the committee cannot drift into an investigation of whatever it finds convenient, power to summon witnesses means the evidence can be tested rather than asserted, and a deadline forces a report while the events are still remembered. What comes out is a set of findings on which the assembly can then decide, and that decision is a separate step. The committee does not try anybody, does not pronounce guilt on a minister, and does not draft the reform, since a report that became legislation on the strength of its own evidence would remove the chamber from the process entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the three features rules out, and what the committee's output actually is.

questions.explanation: Five percent of 1,240,000 is 62,000, because a twentieth is five in every hundred and a hundredth of a million is ten thousand, so a fifth of a hundredth of a million is 62,000. Deducting that from the stated sum leaves 1,178,000, and that is the floor the clause sets for that item. Treating the sum as immovable ignores the reason a statute qualifies an appropriation in the first place, which is to let the executive trim a line without going back to the chamber. Ten percent is double the permitted reduction, and five hundredths of a percent is a hundredth of what is allowed, so each of those figures is excluded by the same arithmetic.

questions.explanation: Two-thirds of 200 is 133 and a third, and 133 votes is 66.5 percent of the chamber, so the smallest whole number that reaches two-thirds is 134, which is 67 percent. A total of 128 clears a bare majority of 101 by 27 votes, which in a chamber that has split looks comfortable, yet it is 6 votes below the figure the clause sets. Half the chamber is 100, which is a different rule, and the sign of the comparison matters as much as its arithmetic: a claim that 128 clears a threshold of 134 is wrong in the same way that its arithmetic is right, since 128 is below 134 and not above it. A parity requirement is a practice of counting, not a consequence of a proportional threshold.

questions.explanation: Recall is an additional remedy, not a substitute one. Between elections the ordinary remedy for an unpopular office-holder is to wait, and recall gives a defined route out that becomes available once a fixed share of the electorate has signed a petition, after which the electorate decides in a vote the office-holder also contests. Nothing in that design turns it into a minority instrument, since the signature threshold filters the initial claim and the deciding vote is a vote like any other, and nothing requires proof of wrongdoing: the question put to voters is about the office-holder, not about a case. Nor does an assembly of any kind decide the outcome, which is the point of the instrument.

questions.explanation: Clemency operates on a case that has run its course, and its object is the penalty rather than the finding of fact. That is why it needs no procedure of proof and no vote: nothing further has to be established, since the conviction stands and only its consequence is addressed. Placing the power in a constitutional office also makes the act an act of the state rather than a direction to a court, and a pardon closes a matter rather than continuing a litigation. It therefore does not follow from a trial but comes after one, is not confined to holders chosen by election, and is not a veto, since a pardon operates on a person and a veto on a text.

questions.explanation: The contribution is continuity. The head of state is not replaced when the government is, so the office supplies something the electoral cycle destroys at each general election: a figure that stands for the state across changes of cabinet and serves no party. That is why the acts described are formal, opening a session, appointing the person the elected politicians have chosen, receiving a foreign representative, and all of them on advice. The same arrangement also removes the office as a check, since a monarch acting on ministerial advice cannot hold up a measure, and it leaves no portfolios, functions or veto behind, since none of the described acts carries a decision of its own.

questions.explanation: The note is a statement about who holds the prerogative, and it is built so that no one person can hold it. If every instrument is the act of the crown rather than a personal act, and the crown acts on the advice of an elected government, then the power travels with the ministry that the assembly can replace and cannot become the private resource of an unelected office-holder. Whether such a rule is enforceable as law or only as convention is a separate question that supporters and critics answer differently, and the note itself does not settle it. What it does settle is that discretion apart from advice, and a government free of the duty to give reasons, are both excluded by its own terms.

stimulus.body: Constitutional practice note, written for this question. Section 4: the sovereign shall act on the advice of the government, and any instrument issued under the prerogative shall be expressed as the act of the crown and shall not be described as the personal act of the sovereign. Section 5: where the sovereign declines to assent to a measure, the reasons shall be laid before the assembly before further business is taken. Section 6: nothing in this note confers on the sovereign the power to act otherwise than on the advice of ministers.

questions.explanation: A casting vote is one additional vote, and its whole effect is on the margin. A motion carried needs one more vote than the motion against it, so in a chamber where the blocs are level the casting vote converts a tie into a win, or a tie into a loss if the holder votes the other way. It does not double anyone's allowance, since one member may not weigh twice, and it is not a veto: the vote carries the measure the holder supports rather than stopping anything, though a holder who always votes against the majority can block as much as a veto holder, which is the honest way to describe the effect. Committee resolution is a different stage and does not make the floor vote idle.

questions.explanation: Two different bodies choose two different offices, and the sizes of those bodies are unconnected. The district electorates together constitute the country, while the national list is a much smaller group, so a head of state can be chosen by a fraction of the voters who choose the legislature. That is the defining feature of the design and the reason it is described as a second, narrower route to the office. It does not create one electorate, since the list electors are a distinct set, and it does not enlarge them, because a list is a smaller body than every district put together; nor does it appoint anybody, since the list electors are chosen in an election and are not delegates appointed by parties.

questions.explanation: A dissolution power that costs the dissolver nothing is cheap, and it is used whenever a president wants a fresh start. Ending the president's own term at the same moment as the assembly's removes that advantage: after sixty days he is a candidate again like anyone else, and the calendar of his own term has restarted. The combination is therefore the price the constitution sets, and it applies whether the assembly is blocked or not, since the effect does not depend on the reason for the dissolution. A new election is not a second beginning for the same office-holder, who must stand for it, and the one-use limit is a separate provision in a later article rather than a consequence of these two.

questions.stem: A constitution lets a president dissolve the assembly on his own initiative, states that the dissolution ends his own term, requires a legislative election within sixty days, and allows the power to be used once in a term. What do the first two provisions together accomplish?

stimulus.body: Constitution extract, written for this question. Article 19: the president of the republic may, on his own initiative, dissolve the national assembly. answer.exemplar: The two relationships give each office-holder a different reason to move towards or away from the chamber, and the difference shows up after an election as well as in daily bargaining. A president with a protected term who wins a legislative majority is in a strong position, because no vote can remove the office-holder and nothing has to be conceded to keep the post. The same protection works the other way, because a president who loses the majority cannot be replaced and is left governing against it until the term ends, which is the situation the literature on these systems calls a cohabitation. A prime minister's position runs the opposite way: the assembly's confidence is needed continuously, so a disagreement about a measure is immediately a disagreement about the ministry and a defeat in a vote can end a government within days. A model answer should treat the two as different incentive structures and should tie the contrast to the moment of an election as well as to day-to-day bargaining, noting that the fixed term insulates the holder at that moment while continuous confidence leaves the assembly master of the ministry.
